stops.stop: Rome, the last emperor the book will name
stops.date_confidence: Terminus post quem only, and the hardest edge the text supplies about itself. Vespasian, who dies in 79, is the latest Roman emperor named anywhere in the Collectanea (29.6), and nothing in the work refers to a later reign. The date marks that limit and nothing else; it is not an event in Solinus's life, of which no source records any. Coordinate is the canonical Rome pin, inherited unchanged from plinio_el_viejo.journey.json.

stops.stop: Rome, the consulship of a stranger
stops.date_confidence: [A] for the consulship, [R] for everything that hangs on it. Marcus Oclatinius Adventus holds his second consulship in 218; that is documented. That he is the 'Adventus' of Solinus's two prefaces is Mommsen's conjecture, adopted by the handbooks, and no ancient source connects the two men. The traditional dating of Solinus rests entirely on this unproved equation.

stops.stop: Rome, a second preface and a second name
stops.date_confidence: Disputed, and the dispute is the point. The older and majority position, in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica and still the default, is that the Polyhistor recension is a sixth-century reworking, not the author's own second edition; English Wikipedia hedges to 'perhaps by Solinus himself'; Hermann Walter's 1969 monograph defends Solinian authorship as the minority view. Von Buren notes that the second dedicatory letter characterizes only Mommsen's third manuscript class. The date orders the segment and asserts nothing.

The quoted French is von Buren's own modern description of the second dedicatory letter, retrieved twice from persee.fr, and not a translation of Solinus's Latin; its context is a sentence about Mommsen's manuscript classes, which is why the letter is described here as a feature of the third class rather than a settled part of the text. Weyman's 1896 review is reported from the dossier and was not re-fetched from the original.

stops.stop: Melbourne, the date moves again
stops.date_confidence: [A] for the dissertation, confirmed at minerva-access.unimelb.edu.au. [R] for its conclusion, which is one scholar's argument from internal evidence and not a new dated witness; it stands against the traditional third-century floruit rather than replacing it. No external document has ever dated the Collectanea, which is why an eighteen-hundred-year-old text can still change centuries.
